spec_choices.why: The designer fixes the game at three seats. The actor rotation, the response step and the split pots all assume exactly three players. With three, bluffing works because a bet must get past two opponents, one of whom may hold the third copy of a rank.
The source has no table talk. The information in play is the actions themselves (check, bet size, call or fold), so adding talk would add a mechanic.

spec_choices.what: Responders are identified by action = CHECK while bet_amount > 0
spec_choices.why: Anyone still showing CHECK once a bet exists must have checked before the bet. Since only one bet is possible, this matches 'each player who checked before the bet'.

spec_choices.what: Score computed for everyone, but published only at a showdown with 2 or more players
spec_choices.why: This keeps the arithmetic uniform while honoring the rule that folded hands and uncontested winners' hands are never revealed.

A thoughtful player weighs the visible board against their hole cards, bets 4 with strong pairs or matches, uses bet size and position to bluff, and reads opponents' checks and calls over 36 hands. A thoughtless player calls or bets blindly.

simplifications.what: Ante, bets and calls are tracked in `paid`, and the net change is applied to `total` at the end of the hand
simplifications.why: This is arithmetically the same as paying at once, and it keeps fractional split pots exact.

variation.original_summary: Greek hold 'em is a poker variant. Each player holds two private hole cards and must use both of them with exactly three of five community cards, with Texas hold 'em style betting rounds between the board stages. The previous XColos adaptation, Greek Hold 'em Mini, cut it to three players, an 18-card numeric deck, 12 hands, a simultaneous 0/1/2 opening bet, a simultaneous FOLD/CALL/RAISE decision after the whole board was visible, and a raise response.

review.evidence: No simple policy dominates. Always-raise gets called by strong hands, and never-fold pays off value bets. Seats were symmetric because all decisions were simultaneous, and choices do change pots.

Over 12 hands, σ ≈ 14 chips against a realistic skill edge of 4-6 chips gives edge/σ ≈ 0.3-0.4. A skilled player wins about 40-45% against two weaker players, versus 33% by chance. Card luck decides most games.

With every board card visible before the main decision, each player knew their exact final score. Good play collapses to fixed strength thresholds that a competent model finds quickly, leaving little to improve beyond that.
Opponents' hole cards were hidden, but the simultaneous decision made bluff raises almost never win a fold, so reads hardly changed outcomes. The payoff to inference was small next to the shuffle.
Hand scores follow from a stated formula, and pots and totals are plain arithmetic. No judge is needed.
It is text-only and turn-based, with one shuffle per hand, a small numeric deck and no board geometry. It fits within the step and attribute limits.

problems: P1: Luck swamps skill. 12 hands is too few, and edge/σ ≈ 0.35 means the deal decides most games.

P2: No uncertainty at the decision. All four board cards were visible before the main bet, so each player knew their exact score and the only open question was opponents' hole cards. Play reduced to fixed thresholds.
P3: Bets had no fold equity. The decision was simultaneous and the raise of 2 was small against the pot, so bluffs almost never won a fold and raising was value-only.
P4: No positional or sequential information. Nobody acted after seeing what others did within a betting round, so opponent modelling had little to work with.
P5: The talk step cost time and steps but added little. Claims are free and unverifiable, and the bets themselves already carry the signal.
P6: The carry rule (all three fold) and the multi-stage opening-bet-then-raise structure added steps and edge cases without adding decisions worth making.

changes.why: Per-game edge/σ grows with the square root of the number of hands, about 1.7× from length alone. Combined with the larger per-hand edge from the other changes, a skilled player should be clearly favoured. Duplicate dealing was rejected because replaying a shuffle with rotated hole hands tells players the other hands they held earlier, which leaks hidden information.

changes.what: Only board cards 1-3 are face up when betting; board card 4 stays face down until showdown.
changes.why: A hand can still gain 4 points if card 4 matches, so draws, card-removal reasoning and bluffing against possible improvement all matter. Hand strength is no longer certain.

changes.what: Replace the simultaneous opening bet and FOLD/CALL/RAISE decision with one sequential betting round. Each player, in an order that rotates each hand, chooses CHECK, BET 2 or BET 4 until someone bets. Later players then CALL or FOLD, and players who checked earlier respond with CALL or FOLD.
changes.why: A bet of 2 or 4 into a pot of 3 gives real fold equity. A bluff of 4 needs both others to fold only about 57% of the time, and a bluff of 2 about 40%. Players act on others' visible actions. Bet sizing becomes a signal that can be honest or deceptive. Check-then-call traps and stealing from the last seat become real options.

changes.what: The first actor rotates every hand, so each seat acts first 12 times, second 12 times and last 12 times.
changes.why: Sequential order creates positional information to exploit, and the rotation keeps seats balanced.
In this zero-sum poker game talk is cheap and unverifiable. Bets already serve as costly, credible communication. Dropping talk shortens a 36-hand game and saves steps.

changes.what: Remove the carry and the separate raise stage. Because a bettor can never fold, the pot always goes to someone.
changes.why: This simplifies the build. The step count per hand falls to 15 and choice steps to at most 4 while keeping every meaningful decision.

keeps: Two private hole cards per player, both of which must be used.
Exactly three board cards count, so a hand scores at most three matches.
Community cards revealed in stages, with betting while some cards are still unknown.
Betting, calling and folding, with the last player in winning without a showdown.
The compact 18-card numeric deck and the established scoring formula, which keep it a game of hand strength, reads and bluffs.

recommendation.reason: The game's core of hidden hole cards, a partly hidden board, and betting with bluff and fold equity is good strategic material. The previous version's flaws (too few hands, no uncertainty at the decision, no fold equity) are fixable within the limits.

variation.name: Greek Hold 'em Mini II
variation.summary: This is a three-player, 36-hand numeric poker game. Each hand has one sequential betting round, played with three board cards visible and a fourth board card still hidden. Bets of 2 or 4 into a pot of 3, a rotating action order and an unseen last card make bluffing, hand-reading and position matter. The longer game lets skill outweigh the shuffle.
variation.rules:
SETUP. Three players, numbered 1, 2 and 3. Each starts with a chip total of 0. Totals may go negative and may include fractions from split pots. The deck has 18 cards: ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, three copies of each, with no suits. The game lasts exactly 36 hands. In hand h, the FIRST ACTOR is player ((h - 1) mod 3) + 1. The SECOND ACTOR is the next player after the first actor (wrapping from 3 to 1), and the THIRD ACTOR is the remaining player.

EACH HAND:
1. Deal. Shuffle all 18 cards; this is the only random event of the hand. Deal 2 hole cards face down to each player and 4 board cards face down to the table. Each player sees only their own hole cards.
2. Ante. Each player pays 1 chip into the pot. The pot starts at 3.
3. Board. Board cards 1, 2 and 3 are turned face up for everyone. Board card 4 stays face down.
4. First actor's choice: CHECK, BET 2 or BET 4. A bet is paid into the pot at once, and the choice is announced to all.
5. Second actor's choice, announced to all. If nobody has bet yet, the choices are CHECK, BET 2 or BET 4. If a bet has been made, the choices are CALL (pay the same amount as the bet into the pot) or FOLD (leave the hand, losing everything already paid).
6. Third actor's choice, with the same options as the second actor, announced to all.
7. Response. This step happens only if a bet was made after at least one player checked. Each player who checked before the bet chooses, at the same moment, CALL (pay the bet amount) or FOLD. The choices are then revealed. Only one bet is ever made in a hand: there are no raises, and the bettor never acts again.
8. Final board. Board card 4 is turned face up.
9. Hand scores. Each player's score is computed from their hole cards (ranks a and b) and the 4 board cards. Score = a + b, plus 6 if a equals b, plus 4 for each match. A match is a board card whose rank equals a or b. At most 3 matches count, because a hand may use only three board cards.
10. Showdown. The players still in the hand are those who did not fold. If exactly one player is still in, that player takes the whole pot and no hole cards are revealed. If two or three are still in, their hole cards and scores are revealed, and the pot goes to the highest score among them. Players tied for the highest score split the pot equally. If everyone checked, all three go to showdown.
11. Folded players' hole cards are never revealed.
12. Totals. Each player's total changes by the chips they won minus the chips they paid this hand. All three totals are announced.
13. All cards return to the deck for the next shuffle.

The sum of all totals is always 0.

END. After hand 36 the game ends.
variation.objective: After 36 hands, the player with the highest chip total wins. If two or three players share the highest total, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
Players can no longer know their exact score when they bet. Card 4 can add 4 points, so paired-with-board hands and hands needing a match play differently. Bets now carry real fold equity: a 4-chip bluff into 3 needs folds only about 57% of the time. This rewards bluffing, check-calling traps, stealing from the third seat after two checks, and reading bet size as a strength signal. Position rotates, so no seat is favoured.

Simple policies all lose. Always-check/always-call gets value-bet without ever winning folds. Always-bet-4/always-call bleeds chips when strong hands call. Always-fold-to-bets is stolen from every hand. Random play loses to all of these.

So the outcome is not decided by the deal when everyone plays well. Even when all three play sensible threshold strategies, sequential bets with a hidden last card mean a player who reads opponents' bet sizes and frequencies, and adjusts bluffing to who still has to act, should gain more than a pure threshold player. A rough estimate is a skill edge of 0.5-0.8 chips per hand, about 18-29 over the game, against σ ≈ 20, for about a 55-65% win rate against two weaker players. This should be confirmed by 3-player simulation.

The chip lead also creates multi-hand planning. A leader late in the game can tighten up, but the ante makes passivity costly. Trailing players must take calculated risks.

Talk is left out. Bets are the costly, credible signals here. Free messages in a zero-sum poker game would only add words, so they fail the reasoning test even though interests conflict.

balanced.evidence:
SCORES: non-pair = a+b+4m (m capped at 3); pair = 2a+6+4m. A pair can have at most one match, because only 3 copies of each rank exist. Ranges: worst 1+2 = 3; best non-pair 5,6 with 3 matches = 11+12 = 23; best pair 6,6 with 1 match = 12+6+4 = 22. After board cards 3 and 4 are shown, each player knows their own score exactly. Only the opponents' scores are unknown.

PAIRWISE LAYER, one pair, my stake s against your stake t: if I score higher I gain min(s,t); if lower I lose min(s,t); if equal, 0. Example table with p = P(I score higher), excluding ties:
- s=0: expected gain 0 against any t.
- s=2, t=0: 0.
- s=2, t=2: 2(2p-1).
- s=4, t=4: 4(2p-1).
- s=4, t=1: 1(2p-1).
No option is strictly better for every opponent action, because the right stake depends on p.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule:
(a) Always stake 4. Sensible opponents stake high only when strong. The always-4 player then loses up to 4 per opponent when behind and wins about 0 when ahead. It is clearly exploitable and loses, which is fine.
(b) Always stake 0. Its pairwise result is identically 0 every hand whatever anyone does, so it cannot be exploited at all. Its total is pure ante-pot luck. Per hand the ante pot gives the winner +6 (prob 1/3) and each loser -3 (prob 2/3), mean 0, sd about 4.24. Over 10 hands the sd is about 13.4.

Now take two sensible players and one always-0 player. The pairwise game between the two sensible players is symmetric and zero-sum, so each expects 0 from it. The always-0 player also expects 0. All three therefore have identical expected totals, and the always-0 player wins about 1/3 of games, the same as correct play. Skilful staking earns nothing over the 'always pass' policy unless an opponent blunders. Under the min(stakes) rule, anyone can opt out of the reasoning layer at zero cost.

There is also no fold, so a bluff can never win the ante pot. A bluff can only lose stake, which makes deception strictly worse than honest staking.

Seats: fully symmetric and simultaneous, so there is no seat edge. All players can win.

The game fails because the thoughtless 'always pass' policy is unexploitable and matches sensible play in expectation.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete and arithmetic:
- The deck, deal, ante, stake bounds (0-2 twice), score formula with match cap, ante-pot tie splits (4.5 / 3) and pairwise settlement are all specified.
- The game is finite at 10 hands. The winner is the highest total, with shared highest a draw.
- One shuffle per hand is the single random draw.
- Hidden elements are 2 (hole cards, face-down board).

Against the limits:
- steps 17 ≤ 20; choice steps 3 ≤ 4; attributes 14 ≤ 20; rounds 10 ≤ 40.
- The deal uses the shared_deck_draw workaround: 10 card moves by remove/append. It plus 3 pairwise steps and the tie-handling ante step fit 17-20 only if per-player operations are grouped within steps. That is tight but plausible.
- No board, judge or clock is needed. All choices are simultaneous polls.

Talk: interests conflict, because every chip moves zero-sum. Talk is simultaneous and placed before stake 2, where a message could push an opponent to stake high into a stronger hand. Talk is justified in principle, though its value is weakened by the balance problem.

No cooperation or betrayal dynamic arises, so there is no late-round collapse.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
With no fold, the 9-chip ante pot goes to the best card score every hand. That alone gives an outcome sd of about 13.4 chips over 10 hands, decided entirely by the deal.

Under the intended good strategy (stake rising with your own score, lowered when opponents' first stakes signal strength), chips flow in the pairwise layer as min(stakes) toward the better hand. That is again card strength.

So when all three play well, both the pot and the transfers go to whoever was dealt better hands, and the winner is decided by the shuffle.

Skill shows only against a player who stakes high when weak. Even then, the always-0 shield gives a non-reasoner the same expectation as a reasoner. There is some inference, from announced first stakes and talk, but no way to turn it into winning a hand you would otherwise lose. You can only shrink or enlarge a transfer that the cards have already decided. Rough estimate: over 80% of the result among competent players is chance.

required_changes: Add a fold decision: at stake 2, players may fold. Folders forfeit their ante and stakes and cannot win the pot. The ante pot goes to the best score among non-folders, and a lone non-folder wins it without comparison. This makes bluffing and reading signals able to win hands the cards would lose.

Replace the min(stakes) pairwise rule with stakes paid into a common pot. Each player pays their full stake, and the pot goes to the best remaining hand. Staking 0 then forfeits pot equity and is no longer an unexploitable shield.

Require staying in to cost something. For example, a player who does not fold must stake at least the highest first stake announced, or fold. This forces a real call/fold decision against inferred strength.

To cut deal luck, consider 15+ hands or a smaller ante relative to the stakes. Then verify that 'always 0 / always fold', 'always max' and random staking each lose clearly to a sensible strategy over a full game.

balanced.evidence:
Stated numbers check out. A non-pair 6+5 with 3 matches scores 11+12=23. A pair of sixes scores 12+6+4=22. 1+2 with no match scores 3. So the range 3-23 is correct, and the claim that a pair has at most one match is correct because only 3 copies of each rank exist.

Maximum outlay per player per hand: ante 1 + open 2 = 3, then call to H=2 (+0) and raise (+2), or call the raise (+2). Total 5. Pot at most 15 + carry.

Thoughtless policies, applying the winner rule:
(a) Always FOLD at step 8: loses the ante plus the open every hand. The only exception is when all three fold, and then the pot carries over rather than returning. The total is certainly negative, about -12 or worse, while a sensible player's total is roughly zero or better. Loses almost always.
(b) Always open 2, always RAISE: the response step costs a caller 2 into a pot of at least 3+2+opens+2, which is 9 or more. Pot odds of about 2:11 mean callers need only about 15% equity, so they almost never fold. The raise therefore buys little fold equity. The maniac holds the best of three random hands about 1/3 of the time but pays the maximum 5 every hand. Openings and showdown cards are revealed, so sensible players learn to call wider with medium hands. Against random play, which folds about 1/3 at step 8 and 1/2 at step 10, the maniac collects folds and wins more often than not. Against sensible play it wins roughly 25-35% of 12-hand games and frequently finishes last. It does not win or draw almost every time.
(c) Always CALL, never fold, open 0: H is set by others, so the call costs at most 2. Facing pot odds of about 2:7, this is correct for roughly the top 75-80% of hands. Calling every time bleeds EV with the bottom hands, and it often loses to selective play. It is not never-losing.
(d) Always open 0, call or fold by threshold: this is a reasonable strategy, not a dominant one.

No option at any step is strictly better whatever the opponents do. FOLD beats CALL with a hand that is certain to lose, and CALL or RAISE beats FOLD with a strong hand.

Seats: all choices are simultaneous polls, information is symmetric and there is no button, so there is no move-order edge. All three players can realistically win, and ties draw.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete. They cover the deal, the ante plus carry, the staged board, the simultaneous open, H, and FOLD/CALL/RAISE amounts. The response step runs only when at least one RAISE and at least one CALL exist, and is a single step with a `when` condition, which is supported. They also cover equal payments by multiple raisers, the showdown with equal split, the uncontested pot, the all-fold carry and its removal in hand 12, and the totals.

Edge cases checked:
- One raises, two fold: no response step; the raiser takes the pot.
- All raise: no response step; showdown.
- Raise, call, fold: the caller responds.

Scoring is pure arithmetic on stored values: a+b, +6 if a=b, +4*min(3, matches). It is finite at 12 hands.

Limits:
- steps 15 ≤ 20
- choice steps 4 ≤ 4 (open, talk, decision, response)
- attributes 17 ≤ 20, plausible: 3 totals, 3 paid-this-hand, 3 in-hand flags, 3 scores, pot, carry, H, plus spares
- hidden elements 2 ≤ 3 (hole cards, unturned board)
- 1 shuffle per hand ≤ 1
- rounds 12 ≤ 40

The showdown max uses the arithmetic_ranking workaround (calc), which is allowed. No board, judge or clock is needed.

Talk is simultaneous and placed before the decision. The game is zero-sum, so players disagree. A message such as 'I'm raising' could induce folds that cost the reader. Talk also gives material for reasoning (consistency with opening bets) and allows two players to try to squeeze the third. This is acceptable.

The fixed-length cooperation test is not relevant, since the game is not a cooperative dilemma.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Once board cards 3-4 are turned, each player knows their exact final score. The only unknown is the 2 opponents' hole cards. The decision tree is very shallow: one open from {0,1,2}, one simultaneous FOLD/CALL/RAISE, and one CALL/FOLD response.

Because the decision is simultaneous and the response faces about 15% pot-odds thresholds, bluff raises almost never generate folds. Raising is essentially value-only, and good play collapses to near-fixed strength thresholds that any competent model finds quickly. There is little room for opponent modelling to change outcomes.

Rough variance estimate:
- Per-hand swing for a contested player: ±4-5 chips, so σ ≈ 4 per hand and ≈ 14 over 12 hands.
- Realistic skill edge of a good player over a mediocre one: about 0.3-0.5 chips per hand, or 4-6 over the game.
- Edge/σ ≈ 0.3-0.4, giving a skilled player roughly 40-45% to win against two weaker players versus a 33% baseline.

That is not clearly favoured, and card luck decides most games. When all three play the intended threshold strategy, the result is decided purely by which player is dealt the best hands across 12 deals. Good play cannot overcome a bad deal here.

There is something to infer (opening bets made after seeing half the board, card removal from the 18-card deck, talk). But the payoff to that inference is small relative to the shuffle.

required_changes: Reduce card luck structurally. Either (a) play 36 hands (within the 40 limit) so the per-game edge/σ roughly doubles, or (b) use duplicate dealing: store each shuffle and replay it for 3 consecutive hands with hole hands rotated among seats, so each player plays every hand once. This needs list attributes within the 20 limit.

Keep real uncertainty at the decision. Turn only board card 3 before step 7/8 and reveal board card 4 at showdown, so scores are not fully known when deciding and both bluffing and hand-reading matter.

Give raises fold equity. Make the raise 4 instead of 2, and/or make the step-8 decision sequential in a seat order that rotates each hand. Raises then come before others act, players respond with information, and opponent modelling is rewarded beyond fixed hand-strength thresholds.

After the changes, re-verify that always-open-2/always-raise and never-fold still lose most games to sensible play, and that a threshold-plus-reading player beats a pure threshold player clearly (e.g. ≥55% in 3-player simulation).

balanced.evidence:
SEAT BALANCE. The first actor in hand h is ((h-1) mod 3)+1. 36 is divisible by 3, so each player is first, second and third actor exactly 12 times. Information is symmetric: everyone sees the same 3 board cards and only their own hole cards. Within a hand, acting last is an advantage, but the rotation shares it out evenly. No seat has a structural edge.

THE MAIN DECISION. The ante pot is 3.
- An uncalled bet of B nets the bettor +2: they paid 1+B and take back 3+B.
- A caller facing a bet of 4 with one player still to act pays 4 into a pot of 7. They need about 36% equity heads-up, more if a third player may call.
- A calling range of roughly the top half of hands is therefore sensible against a bettor who bets every hand.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, applying the winner rule (highest total after 36 hands):
(a) Always first option (CHECK when unbet, CALL when facing a bet). Against sensible play: it never value-bets, so it never wins extra from its strong hands. It also pays 2 or 4 to call every value bet. A sensible player who bets only the top ~30% of hands wins about 4 chips each time from the station's weak calls. Over 36 hands that is a net loss of roughly 15 to 30 chips, so it loses. Against random play it can win, because random folding and bluffing feed it. It does not win or draw almost every time.
(b) Always last option or always highest bid (BET 4 whenever possible, FOLD when facing a bet). As first actor it bets 4 with a random hand. Sensible opponents each call with about the top half of hands, so both fold only about 25% of the time (+2 to the bettor). When called, a random hand against a top-half hand loses about 65 to 70% of showdowns, costing about 5 each time. Expected value is clearly negative. In seats 2 and 3 it folds its ante to every bet. It loses.
(c) Always pass (CHECK, FOLD to any bet). It never wins a contested pot. It loses its 1-chip ante every time anyone bets. Sensible players will bet into it whenever it checks, so it drifts steadily negative and loses.

OTHER CHECKS.
- No option is strictly dominant. BET 2 versus BET 4 trades fold equity against price. CHECK protects weak hands. CALL or FOLD depends on hand strength and on what you read from the bettor.
- The score is described only as an arithmetic score, never labelled as poker ranks, so there is no mislabelled payoff ordering. A pair of 1s scores 8, which a 5-6 (11) beats; that is consistent with the stated formula.
- All three players can realistically win.
- The game is zero-sum; the totals always sum to 0.
- There is no cooperation structure that a safe option could make pointless.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS. Every branch of the betting is defined.
- Unbet: CHECK, BET 2 or BET 4.
- Facing a bet: CALL or FOLD.
- A bet after one or more checks: the earlier checkers answer in a simultaneous poll (correct for a same-moment choice).
- One bet per hand, no raises, and the bettor never acts again.
- If everyone checks, all three go to showdown.
- If one player is left, they take the pot without showing.
- Ties split equally, and fractions are explicitly allowed.

SCORING. The formula is fully arithmetic: a+b, +6 for a pair, +4 per matching board card, at most 3 matches. With three copies of each rank, a pocket pair can match at most one board card, so there is no edge case left open.

FINITENESS. The game is exactly 36 hands. The winner is the highest total, with a draw if the top total is shared. Everything is decided from numbers the game keeps; no judge, board or clock is needed.

LIMITS. All stated figures are within the platform caps:

| Measure | Stated | Cap |
|---|---|---|
| steps_per_round | 15 | 20 |
| choice_steps_per_round | 4 (first, second, third, response) | 4 |
| attributes | 18 | 20 |
| hidden_elements | 2 (hole cards, board card 4) | 3 |
| random_draws_per_round | 1 (one shuffle) | 1 |
| rounds | 36 | 40 |

The deal can be done with the shared_deck_draw workaround (remove/append operations from an 18-card list). The steps stay flat; conditional steps use single `when` conditions.

TALK. With 3 players there is no talk phase, and that is sensible. Interests are strictly opposed and there is nothing to propose or coordinate on, so talk would be cheap and unenforceable. Players already signal and read each other through check, bet size, call and fold, so they are not left only guessing.

REPEATED-GAME CLAUSE. The cooperation-after-betrayal clause does not apply: this is a competitive betting game, not a cooperation game.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THERE IS TO INFER.
- By the time you bet you know 5 of the 18 cards and your score except for board card 4.
- A needed rank with k unseen copies arrives as card 4 with probability k/13, worth +4.
- Opponents' hole cards are hidden. They must be inferred from card removal and from their action: check, bet 2, bet 4, call or fold, and their position.
- Over 36 hands, revealed showdown hands let a player learn each opponent's bluffing and calling thresholds.
- Players can act on those inferences through bet sizing, bluffs, folds and the simultaneous call/fold response.

CHANCE ESTIMATE.
- Per-hand net swing has a standard deviation of roughly 3 chips. An all-check hand is +2/-1/-1 (SD about 1.4); bet hands swing up to ±8.
- Over 36 hands, a player's total has an SD of about 18 and the gap between two players about 25.
- A good player's edge over naive play (a calling station, or random or always-bet play) is about 0.7 to 1 chip per hand, roughly 25 to 36 chips. That is 1 to 1.5 SD, so the reasoner wins most games against such opponents.
- Against competent but imperfect opponents the edge is smaller, about 0.3 chips per hand. That still clearly lifts the reasoner above the 1/3 base rate.
- Chance plays a substantial but minority role.

WHEN ALL PLAY WELL. If every player follows the intended good strategy, the winner depends on the cards. However, no single hidden type or deal fixes the result: a bad hand can be folded for 1 chip, and a weak hand can steal a pot by betting. A good player can therefore overcome a poor run of deals.

triage.reason: The file works as specified, but the betting structure lets a mindless policy dominate: always taking the last option (bet the maximum 4, never back down) wins 56 of 60 games from seat 1. Opponents who are uncertain fold often and hand over the pot, so raw aggression beats any judgment of card strength.
triage.guidance:
Rebalance the betting so that always betting the maximum is not a dominant strategy. Options:
(1) Remove the fold option. Every player still in the hand matches H, possibly all-in, and the showdown always decides. Bets then raise the stakes but cannot win pots alone, so card strength matters.
(2) Alternatively, make folding cheap and over-betting costly. For example, a folder recovers half of what they bet, or the highest bettor's excess over the second-highest bet is returned and not at risk.
(3) Shrink the bet range, for example 0–2, and increase the ante or the pair and match weights so the showdown dominates the outcome.
(4) Order the options so that 'last' is not automatically the most aggressive choice.
Then re-run the thoughtless-policy checks: first and last at each seat should win at roughly the random rate. Also check that seat 1 has no edge.
